case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress, through the Bankruptcy Code’s definition of “governmental unit” and its sovereign-immunity abrogation clause, unequivocally abrogated federally recognized Indian tribes’ sovereign immunity from suit in bankruptcy proceedings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 106(a) (abrogation of sovereign immunity as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions), read with 11 U.S.C. § 101(27) (definition of “governmental unit” including “foreign or domestic government[s]”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Lac du Flambeau Band and its tribal business entities argue that tribal sovereign immunity is a core attribute of tribal sovereignty and can be displaced only by Congress with an unequivocal, clear textual statement. Because the Bankruptcy Code does not mention “Indian tribes” (or equivalent unmistakable language) in § 106(a) or § 101(27), it does not satisfy the Supreme Court’s clear-statement rule for abrogating tribal immunity. The First Circuit’s reliance on policy considerations, functional comparisons, and “historical context” improperly substituted for the required explicit statutory expression, threatened tribal self-governance by exposing tribes to litigation burdens (including discovery), and intruded on Congress’s exclusive authority to set federal Indian policy.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Coughlin argues that § 106(a) expressly abrogates the sovereign immunity of any “governmental unit” for the listed bankruptcy provisions, and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” broadly to include “foreign or domestic government[s],” which encompasses Indian tribes as domestic sovereign governments. Under the Court’s abrogation cases, Congress need not use the word “tribe” so long as the statutory text clearly captures the sovereign category at issue. He also emphasizes the First Circuit’s reasoning that tribes often function like other governmental units in bankruptcy (e.g., tax-related provisions) and contends the case posture is interlocutory and would benefit from further percolation, though he concedes an “irreconcilable” circuit split exists.
key_precedents: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, 30 U.S. (5 Pet.) 1 (1831)
Meyers v. Oneida Tribe of Indians of Wisconsin, 836 F.3d 818 (7th Cir. 2016)
Krystal Energy Co. v. Navajo Nation, 357 F.3d 1055 (9th Cir. 2004)
In re Greektown Holdings, LLC (6th Cir. decision holding no abrogation of tribal immunity in bankruptcy)
Penobscot Nation v. Frey, 3 F.4th 484 (1st Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point has force, especially under Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills, but it reads the canon as a near magic-words rule. Here Congress did not abrogate by implication: § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s definition covering any “foreign or domestic government” is a categorical identification that, on ordinary meaning, includes tribes as domestic sovereigns. As Justice Kagan notes, excluding tribes would require an atextual carveout from a comprehensive definition, which is the less minimalist move because it narrows enacted text without a textual hook. The narrow, institution-protective disposition is simply to hold that tribes fall within “domestic government” in § 101(27) for purposes of § 106(a), leaving any tribal-specific exemption to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: that “foreign or domestic government” in § 101(27) has an ordinary meaning broad enough to include tribes, and that excluding tribes would be an atextual carveout. But the clear-statement rule in Santa Clara Pueblo and reinforced by Bay Mills is not satisfied by a residual, catchall category that reaches tribes only as a possible implication—especially where Congress elsewhere speaks directly of “Indian tribes” when it wishes to displace tribal sovereign prerogatives. Section 106(a) is “express” only as to “governmental unit,” so the dispositive question is whether the definition unmistakably identifies tribes, and the conspicuous omission of any tribal referent amid a detailed list of entities cuts against that conclusion under a strict textualist/originalist approach. Uniformity concerns in bankruptcy (emphasized by Justice Alito) cannot supply the unequivocal abrogation that the enacted text lacks.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point is the best for petitioner: Congress did not say “Indian tribe,” and Bay Mills/Santa Clara Pueblo caution against assuming abrogation. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the canon demands unmistakable coverage, not magic words, and §§ 106(a) and 101(27) work together to abrogate immunity for a defined class—“governmental unit”—that expressly includes any “foreign or domestic government,” which in ordinary usage encompasses tribes as domestic sovereigns. Reading tribes out of “domestic government” would be an atextual carveout that rewrites a categorical definition Congress chose, and it would impair core bankruptcy tools like the stay in ways Congress likely sought to avoid through uniform administration. Bay Mills reinforces caution, but it does not authorize narrowing an express abrogation plus broad sovereign definition into a tribe-only exception absent statutory text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist—under Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills—on an unequivocal abrogation, but his approach effectively converts that clarity requirement into a magic-words rule demanding Congress say “Indian tribe.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” plainly covers tribes as domestic sovereigns; excluding them would be an atextual carveout. Bay Mills cautions against lightly assuming Congress curtailed tribal self-government, but here Congress spoke in categorical sovereign terms that preserve bankruptcy’s uniform, debtor-protective mechanisms—especially important for vulnerable debtors who depend on the stay and discharge. Nothing in the precedents undermines applying an express abrogation provision to a class definition that unmistakably reaches the sovereign at issue.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point, grounded in Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills, is the best argument for petitioner, but it treats the canon as a magic-words rule rather than a demand for unmistakable coverage. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” is a categorical sovereign-facing definition that, on ordinary legal usage, encompasses federally recognized tribes as domestic governments. Reading tribes out would require an atextual carveout that disrupts the Bankruptcy Code’s coherent, uniform operation (e.g., stay enforcement and turnover) and is less faithful to the enacted text than applying the definition as written. Bay Mills cautions against inference, but here the abrogation is explicit and the coverage comes from Congress’s own definitional choice, which is sufficiently unequivocal under a pragmatic textualist approach.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Santa Clara Pueblo/Bay Mills point presses the canon as far as it can go, but it still does not justify converting an “unequivocal expression” requirement into a magic-words rule demanding “Indian tribe.” As the Chief Justice notes, § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” is a categorical identification of sovereigns that, in ordinary legal usage, encompasses federally recognized tribes as domestic governments. Treating tribes as excluded would require an atextual carveout from Congress’s comprehensive definition—precisely the sort of judicial rewriting a textualist methodology should avoid. Bay Mills cautions against lightly assuming abrogation by implication, but here the abrogation is explicit in § 106(a) and the scope is supplied by the enacted definition, not inference.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills require an “unequivocal” abrogation and Congress did not say “tribe,” but that canon does not impose a magic-words requirement; it asks whether the statute unmistakably covers the sovereign. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” is a categorical sovereign definition that, in ordinary legal usage, includes federally recognized tribes as domestic sovereigns—excluding them would require an atextual carveout. Bay Mills cautions against lightly inferring abrogation, but here the abrogation is explicit and the coverage is supplied by Congress’s enacted definition rather than implication. The administrability and uniformity concerns Roberts highlights in the bankruptcy context further support adhering to the statutory line Congress drew rather than crafting a judicial exception.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to foreground Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills: abrogation must be “unequivocally expressed,” and Congress’s omission of the word “tribe” is not trivial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the clear-statement rule is satisfied by unmistakable categorical coverage, not by magic words, and § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” a term Congress then defined to include any “foreign or domestic government.” Textually, tribes are domestic sovereign governments, so applying that definition is not an implication-based abrogation but a straightforward application of enacted terms; carving tribes out would be an atextual exception inconsistent with the statute’s comprehensive design. Bay Mills’ caution against lightly assuming abrogation is met here because Congress spoke directly through an explicit abrogation provision plus a sovereign-encompassing definition, even if it did not enumerate every sovereign by name.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clearest argument is that Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills require an “unequivocal” statement and that Congress did not say “Indian tribe,” but that would convert the clear-statement rule into a magic-words requirement rather than a demand for unmistakable coverage. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 106(a) is an express abrogation keyed to “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines that term to include any “foreign or domestic government,” which—on ordinary meaning and in legal usage—naturally encompasses tribes as domestic sovereigns without any atextual carveout. Bay Mills’ caution against lightly assuming abrogation is satisfied here because the abrogation is explicit and the coverage comes from a categorical sovereign definition Congress enacted, not from inference or judicial policy. Given the practical consequences for uniform bankruptcy administration (stay enforcement, turnover, discharge-related remedies), I do not see a doctrinally sound basis to exclude tribes absent a textual exception Congress did not write.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 106(a) abrogates sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit” as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions, and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include any “foreign or domestic government,” language broad enough to encompass federally recognized Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns. While Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez requires that abrogation of tribal immunity be “unequivocally expressed,” that clear-statement rule is satisfied when Congress clearly identifies the sovereign category it is reaching, even if it does not use the word “tribe,” and here Congress used an expansive definition coupled with an express abrogation clause. Given the need for a workable, uniform bankruptcy system and the statutory text Congress chose, the narrower, institutionally stabilizing course is to read the Code as abrogating immunity for all entities captured by § 101(27), leaving any tribal-specific carveout to Congress. This approach respects precedent by applying the same clear-statement framework used in Bay Mills and C & L Enterprises, while grounding the decision in the enacted text rather than policy improvisation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Tribal sovereign immunity may be abrogated only when Congress "unequivocally expressed" that intent, and the Bankruptcy Code nowhere mentions "Indian tribes" in either § 106(a) or the definitional cross-reference in § 101(27). Reading § 101(27)’s general phrase "foreign or domestic government[s]" to include tribes would dilute the clear-statement rule and effectively permit abrogation by implication, contrary to Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez, 436 U.S. 49, 58 (1978), and Bay Mills’ admonition that courts will not lightly assume Congress meant to undermine tribal self-government. Textually, § 106(a) abrogates immunity only for a "governmental unit" as defined, and nothing in § 101(27) uses unmistakable language that captures tribes as sovereigns subject to suit in bankruptcy. Because Congress knows how to speak clearly when it intends to subject tribes to federal-court litigation, I would not extend § 106(a) to tribes absent an express statutory statement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 106(a) unequivocally abrogates sovereign immunity as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government,” language that naturally encompasses federally recognized Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns. The clear-statement rule requires that Congress speak unmistakably, not that it recite a magic word like “tribe,” and the combination of §§ 106(a) and 101(27) is sufficiently categorical in covering sovereign governments. Reading the statute otherwise would create a significant practical gap in the uniform operation of bankruptcy law by allowing tribes (and their instrumentalities) to evade core bankruptcy mechanisms to which other sovereign creditors and regulators are subject. Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez confirms the need for an unequivocal expression of abrogation, and here Congress supplied it through a broad, all-sovereigns definition coupled with an express abrogation clause.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 106(a) abrogates sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines that term to include any “foreign or domestic government,” a textual category that naturally encompasses federally recognized Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns. While Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez and Bay Mills require that abrogation be “unequivocally expressed,” that clear-statement rule is satisfied when Congress clearly names the sovereign class it is regulating, even if it does not use the word “tribe,” and here the Code’s breadth is reinforced by Congress’s evident aim to make core bankruptcy remedies (like the automatic stay and discharge-related provisions incorporated via § 106(a)) effective against governmental creditors. Reading tribes out of “domestic government” would create a practical loophole that undermines uniform bankruptcy relief and disproportionately harms financially distressed debtors, for whom the stay’s protection is often essential to basic stability and access to a meaningful fresh start. Given Congress’s broad remedial design in bankruptcy and the statute’s express abrogation mechanism, the better reading is that tribes are covered as “governmental unit[s]” under §§ 106(a) and 101(27).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 106(a) unequivocally abrogates the sovereign immunity of any “governmental unit” for a long list of Bankruptcy Code provisions, and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government.” Given that federally recognized tribes are domestic sovereign governments, that categorical text most naturally includes them, and the clear-statement rule does not require Congress to use the word “tribe” if the statutory category plainly covers the sovereign in question. Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez requires an unequivocal expression, but it treats the rule as a canon of construction rather than a magic-words requirement, and here the abrogation clause plus the broad definition operates coherently and workably across the Code’s bankruptcy scheme. Reading tribes out of “domestic government” would create an atextual carveout from § 106(a)’s comprehensive abrogation and undermine uniform bankruptcy administration where governmental creditors and regulators are routinely bound by core bankruptcy provisions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 106(a) expressly abrogates the sovereign immunity of any “governmental unit” for specified Bankruptcy Code provisions, and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government.” As a matter of ordinary meaning, federally recognized Indian tribes are domestic sovereign governments, so the text Congress chose captures them without needing the magic words “Indian tribe.” The clear-statement rule from Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez requires that abrogation be “unequivocally expressed,” but it does not demand a particular label when the statutory category plainly encompasses the sovereign at issue. Reading §§ 106(a) and 101(27) together, Congress spoke with sufficient clarity to abrogate tribal immunity in bankruptcy, and it is not the Court’s role to narrow that broad textual choice based on policy concerns about tribal self-governance.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 106(a) abrogates sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include “foreign or domestic government[s],” a category that naturally encompasses federally recognized Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns. While Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez requires that abrogation of tribal sovereign immunity be “unequivocally expressed,” that clear-statement rule is satisfied when Congress uses broad but precise sovereign categories that plainly capture tribes, not only when it uses the word “tribe.” Reading §§ 106(a) and 101(27) together, the statutory text provides a workable, administrable rule in bankruptcy and avoids creating an atextual immunity carveout that Congress did not write. This interpretation also respects precedent and the Bankruptcy Code’s design for uniform application to governmental creditors and regulators in core bankruptcy proceedings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 106(a) abrogates sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit” as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions, and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government.” Read according to its ordinary public meaning, that catchall encompasses Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns, making Congress’s abrogation sufficiently clear in the text even if it does not use the word “tribe.” The clear-statement rule requires an “unequivocal[] express[ion]” of abrogation, Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez, 436 U.S. 49, 58 (1978), but it does not demand magic words where the statutory category unmistakably includes the sovereign at issue. Given the Bankruptcy Code’s comprehensive scheme and the breadth of §§ 106(a) and 101(27), the better textual reading is that Congress spoke with the requisite clarity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 106(a) expressly abrogates sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit” with respect to enumerated Bankruptcy Code provisions, and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government,” text that naturally encompasses federally recognized Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns. While Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez requires that any abrogation of tribal sovereign immunity be “unequivocally expressed,” that clear-statement rule is satisfied when Congress clearly captures the sovereign category at issue even without naming it, and the Code’s broad, categorical definition paired with an explicit abrogation clause meets that standard. Reading the statute otherwise risks a serious practical consequence: it would create a bankruptcy carveout enabling governmental creditors that are tribes to evade core bankruptcy processes (e.g., turnover, automatic-stay enforcement), undermining procedural fairness and the uniform operation of bankruptcy law. Given Congress’s evident intent in § 106(a) to place all governmental units on the same footing in bankruptcy, the better reading is that tribal immunity is abrogated for the specified provisions.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress, through the Bankruptcy Code’s abrogation of sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit,” clearly and unequivocally abrogated tribal sovereign immunity so that an Indian tribe can be sued in bankruptcy proceedings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 106(a) (abrogation of sovereign immunity for a “governmental unit” as to enumerated Bankruptcy Code provisions), read with 11 U.S.C. § 101(27) (definition of “governmental unit,” including “foreign or domestic government[s]”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the Lac du Flambeau Band and its tribal lending entities) argue that tribal sovereign immunity is a strong, common-law immunity that can be displaced only by an unmistakably clear statement from Congress, and the Bankruptcy Code does not meet that standard because it never mentions “Indian tribes” (or equivalent terms) and “domestic government” is, at most, an ambiguous general label that cannot be treated as an unequivocal abrogation. They contend the First Circuit improperly relied on policy considerations and contextual/historical reasoning rather than the required clear textual expression, and that allowing implied abrogation threatens tribal self-governance and Congress’s primacy in setting federal Indian policy. They also emphasize an acknowledged circuit split and real-world harms from being forced into discovery and litigation despite immunity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (the debtor) argues that § 106(a) expressly abrogates sovereign immunity for all “governmental unit[s],” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of “foreign or domestic government[s]” is clear enough to include Indian tribes as domestic sovereign governments, satisfying the unequivocal-expression requirement without needing the word “tribe.” Respondent further contends Supreme Court review is premature because the case is interlocutory and factual development and alternative grounds for dismissal remain, and suggests further circuit percolation could be useful. Respondent downplays broader implications beyond bankruptcy and disputes that additional, non-bankruptcy conflicts warrant immediate review.
key_precedents: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) (tribes as “domestic dependent nations”)
Cooper v. Aaron (referenced in the First Circuit appendix excerpt for the proposition that a statute need not use particular magic words)
Meyers v. Oneida Tribe of Indians of Wisconsin, 836 F.3d 818 (7th Cir. 2016)
In re Greektown Holdings, LLC (6th Cir.)
Krystal Energy Co. v. Navajo Nation (9th Cir.)
Penobscot Nation v. Frey (1st Cir.) (cited in the appendix excerpt for textual-clarity approach)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills for an “unequivocal” statement, and his point that Congress often names “Indian tribes” elsewhere is a fair warning against loose inference. But here the statute does not ask us to infer abrogation from silence; as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, Congress paired an express abrogation of “sovereign immunity” in § 106(a) with a definition of “governmental unit” that includes any “foreign or domestic government,” and tribes fit comfortably within the ordinary meaning of a domestic sovereign government. Treating “domestic government” as excluding tribes would require us to create an atextual carveout from a carefully integrated definition-plus-abrogation scheme—precisely the kind of judicial narrowing that undermines institutional legitimacy. I would keep the holding narrow, limited to the enumerated § 106(a) provisions and bankruptcy’s core administration, without opining more broadly about tribal authority outside that context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch press the best point—that § 106(a) abrogates immunity for all “governmental unit[s]” and § 101(27)’s “foreign or domestic government” could, in ordinary speech, be broad enough to include tribes. But under Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills, the question is not breadth in the abstract; it is whether Congress unmistakably directed abrogation at the distinct, judge-recognized immunity of Indian tribes, and generic catchall terms are insufficient when Congress routinely and readily names “Indian tribes” when it intends to legislate for them. Treating “domestic government” as necessarily including tribes collapses the sui generis status Cherokee Nation recognized and turns a clear-statement rule into an inference rule—precisely what those cases forbid in the immunity context. The bankruptcy-uniformity concerns Justice Alito raises are policy arguments that cannot supply the missing unequivocal textual focus on tribes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clearest point is that Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills require an “unequivocal” abrogation and that Congress often says “Indian tribes” when it means tribes. But those cases demand unmistakable textual clarity, not a magic-words requirement, and § 106(a)’s express abrogation of “sovereign immunity” for all “governmental unit[s],” coupled with § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government,” is clear enough to reach tribes as domestic sovereigns in ordinary legal usage—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize. Treating tribes as a silent exception would be an atextual carveout that the statute does not supply and would predictably disrupt core bankruptcy mechanisms like the automatic stay, a practical consequence Congress plausibly sought to avoid through categorical drafting. Cherokee Nation’s “domestic dependent nations” label underscores tribes’ sovereign character within the United States, which supports (rather than defeats) fitting them within “domestic government” for purposes of this definitional scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point—grounded in Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills—that Congress must name “Indian tribes” expressly is serious, but it improperly converts “unequivocal” into a magic-words requirement. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 106(a) squarely abrogates “sovereign immunity” for every “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” is a comprehensive definition that, in ordinary usage and in light of our recognition of tribes as sovereign polities within the United States, naturally encompasses tribes without judicially inserting an atextual carveout. Cherokee Nation’s “domestic dependent nations” label underscores tribes’ sovereign character but does not exclude them from being domestic governments for bankruptcy’s definitional purposes. The pragmatic consequences Justice Alito highlights confirm the textual reading: carving tribes out would predictably undermine the automatic stay and discharge in ways Congress enacted § 106(a) to prevent, with concrete harms for debtors and vulnerable creditors who need bankruptcy’s core protections to operate uniformly.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills require an “unequivocal” abrogation and that the Code never says “Indian tribe”—doesn’t overcome the definition-plus-abrogation structure Congress enacted. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 106(a) expressly abrogates “sovereign immunity” for every “governmental unit,” and § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” is categorical language that, in ordinary usage and in our own descriptions of tribes as sovereign domestic polities, clearly encompasses tribes without judicially inventing an atextual carveout. Thomas’s reliance on Congress’s practice of naming tribes elsewhere is, at most, a weak negative inference and cannot trump the operative, integrated definition Congress chose here. Bay Mills reinforces that we demand textual clarity, but it does not impose a magic-words requirement where the enacted definition makes application straightforward.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Santa Clara Pueblo objection is the most serious, but it would convert the clear-statement rule into a magic-words regime that our cases do not adopt: the question is whether Congress’s enacted text unmistakably covers the sovereign, not whether it recites a preferred label. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 106(a) expressly abrogates “sovereign immunity” for every “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines that unit to include any “foreign or domestic government,” a category that, in ordinary legal usage and consistent with our descriptions of tribes as domestic sovereigns, encompasses tribes without any atextual carveout. Bay Mills strengthens the need for textual clarity, but it also confirms Congress can abrogate tribal immunity by statute; here the definition-plus-abrogation structure supplies that clarity. I do not see a methodological basis to narrow “domestic government” to exclude tribes given the statute’s comprehensive language and integrated design.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point is serious, but it effectively converts Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills into a magic-words rule that our cases do not impose: the question is whether Congress has unmistakably expressed abrogation in the enacted text, and § 106(a) expressly abrogates “sovereign immunity” for all “governmental unit[s]” as defined. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 101(27)’s inclusion of any “foreign or domestic government” is comprehensive, sovereignty-inclusive language that, in ordinary legal usage and consistent with our repeated recognition of tribes as domestic sovereign polities, naturally covers tribes without needing the phrase “Indian tribe.” Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan reinforce the key methodological point: excluding tribes would require us to create an atextual carveout from a definition-and-abrogation scheme Congress deliberately drafted categorically rather than as a potentially underinclusive list. Practical bankruptcy consequences (not as a substitute for text, but as a confirmatory backdrop) also support Roberts’s narrow, bankruptcy-bound holding because a tribal exception would destabilize core provisions like the stay and discharge in a way Congress’s categorical drafting seems designed to prevent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest argument—that Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills require Congress to name “Indian tribes” rather than rely on general language—does not, in my view, follow from the text-focused clear-statement rule those cases apply. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 106(a) expressly abrogates “sovereign immunity” as to every “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines that unit to include any “foreign or domestic government,” a comprehensive category whose ordinary public meaning most naturally encompasses tribes as domestic sovereigns. Treating tribes as excluded would require an atextual carveout from an enacted definition, which is harder to justify on originalist and textualist premises than applying the statute’s categorical terms as written. Bay Mills reinforces the need for clarity, but it does not transform that requirement into a magic-words rule when Congress has drafted an integrated definition-plus-abrogation scheme that plainly reaches the sovereign at issue.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that Santa Clara Pueblo and Bay Mills require an “unequivocal” abrogation specifically directed at tribes—properly centers the clear-statement canon, but it still does not justify treating that canon as a magic-words rule. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Congress paired an express abrogation of “sovereign immunity” in § 106(a) with a definition of “governmental unit” that includes any “foreign or domestic government,” and our cases describing tribes as sovereign polities within the United States make the application of that definition textually straightforward. Thomas’s reliance on tribes’ sui generis status (and Congress’s practice of naming tribes elsewhere) is not enough to overcome the enacted definition here; excluding tribes would require an atextual carveout that would predictably disrupt core bankruptcy mechanisms like the automatic stay, a practical consequence that reinforces—not substitutes for—the statutory clarity. Bay Mills affects my analysis only insofar as it reaffirms the clarity requirement, and I think that requirement is met by the Code’s definition-and-abrogation structure without needing the specific phrase “Indian tribe.”

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 106(a) expressly abrogates sovereign immunity as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include “foreign or domestic government[s],” a category that naturally encompasses Indian tribes as domestic sovereigns. Under Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez, abrogation must be “unequivocally expressed,” but that canon does not require “magic words” so long as the text, read in its ordinary sense, makes Congress’s intent clear; here, Congress chose comprehensive, all-sovereign language rather than a list that would invite omissions. A narrow holding limited to the bankruptcy context respects precedent and promotes the uniformity and institutional functioning of the Bankruptcy Code without venturing into broader questions of tribal authority beyond the enumerated provisions in § 106(a).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Tribal sovereign immunity is a background common-law immunity that Congress may abrogate only by an unequivocal textual statement. Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez holds that abrogation of tribal immunity “cannot be implied but must be unequivocally expressed,” and nothing in 11 U.S.C. § 106(a) or the definition of “governmental unit” in 11 U.S.C. § 101(27) mentions “Indian tribes” or uses similarly unmistakable language. The catchall phrase “foreign or domestic government[s]” is too general to satisfy that clear-statement rule for tribes, especially given this Court’s repeated insistence on clear textual expression when displacing sovereign immunity. Because the Code lacks the requisite explicitness, I would not read it to abrogate tribal immunity in bankruptcy proceedings.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 106(a) abrogates sovereign immunity as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government,” language that naturally encompasses an Indian tribe as a domestic sovereign. Under this Court’s cases, abrogation must be “unequivocally expressed,” but that does not require “magic words” so long as the statutory text, read in context, clearly reaches the sovereign at issue. See Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez, 436 U.S. 49, 58–59 (1978), and Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Cmty., 572 U.S. 782, 790 (2014). Given bankruptcy’s need for uniform, comprehensive administration of the estate and the Code’s broad definition, the practical consequences of exempting tribes from core bankruptcy proceedings counsel against reading an unwritten tribal carveout into Congress’s all-encompassing term “domestic government.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 106(a) expressly abrogates sovereign immunity for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines that term to include any “foreign or domestic government,” language that naturally encompasses Indian tribes as sovereigns within the United States (Cherokee Nation v. Georgia). The clear-statement rule from Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez and Bay Mills demands an unequivocal expression, but it does not require “magic words”; Congress can speak clearly through general terms when the category unmistakably includes tribes, and the Bankruptcy Code’s paired provisions do so here. In bankruptcy, a regime designed to centralize claims and provide comprehensive relief, recognizing tribal immunity would create practical gaps that fall hardest on debtors and other vulnerable creditors, undermining uniform administration of the estate. Reading §§ 106(a) and 101(27) together therefore best effectuates Congress’s remedial design while still respecting the canon by requiring a clear textual abrogation, which is present.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 106(a) abrogates sovereign immunity as to specified Bankruptcy Code provisions for any “governmental unit,” and § 101(27) defines “governmental unit” to include a “foreign or domestic government.” Given this Court’s recognition that tribes are sovereigns within the United States—“domestic dependent nations,” Cherokee Nation v. Georgia—an Indian tribe fits most naturally within “domestic government,” and the text thus supplies the requisite unequivocal expression without requiring the statute to say “Indian tribe” as a magic word. Santa Clara Pueblo v. Martinez imposes a clear-statement canon that abrogation cannot be implied, but it remains a tool of interpretation; here, the statute’s broad, categorical abrogation paired with an inclusive definition makes the better reading that Congress spoke clearly enough to reach tribes. That interpretation also promotes the Bankruptcy Code’s workability and coherence by preventing a significant class of domestic sovereign creditors from opting out of core bankruptcy processes Congress made applicable to “governmental units.”
